How the interview runs (sourced)

The Chime SQL interview, as candidates report it

Chime does not publish the format. Each row is what candidates and prep guides have described publicly, with its source; where sources disagree, the row says so. Formats change — treat every specific as reported, not official.

Roles where SQL is testedTwo of the reports are for Data Scientist; a third, for a software engineering role leaning toward data engineering, also had SQL.[1][2][3]
Technical screenOne data scientist report (interview October 2025) describes a technical screen of one hour of SQL and one hour of a business case on a spreadsheet of metrics. The candidate wrote that a fast candidate gets through five or six SQL questions in the hour.[1]
Hiring-manager screenAnother data scientist report (interview November 2025) describes a recruiter screen, then a one-hour hiring-manager screen split in two: 30 minutes on background, 30 minutes writing SQL. The candidate was told Chime no longer gives a take-home and the next step was the virtual onsite.[2]
The dataBoth data scientist reports describe two tables, users and transactions. In the hiring-manager screen no schema was given: the candidate queried the rows first to learn the columns, then had to define a retention metric before writing it.[1][2]
Software engineering roleA report for a software role leaning toward data engineering (October 2025) calls the SQL very basic and says it did not include window functions.[3]
What is not settledAll three are single candidate reports from late 2025. None names the coding tool, and none describes a data analyst loop; no source we could read states one format for every Chime data role. (no reliable source)

  2. [2] PracHub — Chime Data Scientist hiring-manager screen, a retention question with no schema (candidate report, interview Nov 2025) (25 Aug 2026)
  3. [3] PracHub — Chime Software Engineer, basic SQL without window functions (candidate report, Oct 2025) (17 Sep 2026)

The SQL that comes up

What Chime SQL questions test

Reported most often, in order

  • 1Timestamps truncated to a day or month before grouping
  • 2Layered CTEs
  • 3Ranking with ties kept
  • 4Comparing a row with the one before it
  • 5Rolling sums over a window
  • 6Defining a retention metric from users and transactions
  • 7Basic joins and aggregation (the software engineering report)

Difficulty: Reported as medium in the October 2025 technical screen and easy in the November 2025 hiring-manager screen, which ended in a rejection; the software engineering report calls its SQL easy. The data is users and their transactions, with the transaction time stored as a full timestamp.

Sample questions

Chime SQL question shapes, and where to practise them

Shapes candidates and guides report (paraphrased)

  • Users and their transactions, the transaction time a full timestamp: metrics per day or month, which means truncating the timestamp first.[1]
  • The same two tables: rank with ties kept, compare each row with the one before it, and a rolling sum over a window.[1]
  • Users and transactions with no schema given: what early behaviour signals that a user will be retained — define the metric, then write the SQL.[2]

Every challenge in the Chime set, by topic

These are SQL Quest challenges matched to the topics candidates report for Chime — not questions Chime has asked.

Every query here runs on SQLite in your browser. Joins, GROUP BY, CTEs and window functions are written the same way in PostgreSQL, MySQL and Snowflake; dates are where they differ (SQLite's strftime('%Y-%m', ts) is to_char(ts, 'YYYY-MM') in PostgreSQL), and the app lists each difference beside every challenge.
